Title: WwEF: game balance and other cards (long)

Messages.Author: Alan Kwan
Messages.Body:
I have included excrepts of an earlier seller's post (I was
NOT the poster of that one) at the end of this post, for
the purpose of supporting data.

One way, I think, of looking at game balance is like this:
if a popular, hot card is modified by raising its cost,
would people still be using it the same?

Think about WwEF. Some people use more than 10.
If the card costs 1 blood to play, would people still
use it? I think they'll still use 4 or 5. If
it costs 2 blood, would people still use it? Some
may put 1 or 2 in the deck, but the card is not too
terrific at 2 blood. But if someone would still use
1 or 2 (I'd use 1) if the cost is raised by 2, then
it is quite likely that the card is currently too cheap.
Raising its cost by 1 would be quite reasonable, IMO.

On a side note, I think in Revised the card should
only be useable if you are playing another reaction or
are actually blocking (a blockable action at
enough intercept). In other words, no dumping
the card on a bleed across the table or on a
stealthed action without risking combat.

In the commercial quoted below, WwEF is the only
common card which is sold out! The demand for this
card seems to be much higher than some useful
commons, such as Lucky Blow and Computer Hacking,
and the Animalism untaps. The cost of "Do not
Replace until end of Combat" for a /reaction/
(not combat) card simply outweights the
requirement of a discipline (WwEF is also
more flexible than the Animalism untaps).

Another one is Misdirection. If it costs 1+X,
people will no doubt still use it. If it costs
2+X, some people may still use it, but some will
be taking it out of their decks, If it costs
2X, then I bet people will shake their heads and
take it out. So 2X is no doubt too expensive,
but X is simply too cheap. Because there are
Dominate bleeds and the like, 2+X is not
entirely unreasonable.

A card less often talked about is Majesty.
Depending on deck strategy, some players
put 12 or more in their decks. A Strike:
Combat Ends is many things in one. It counters
all strikes, all additional strikes, and all
presses. And if that is not enough, the
Superior version allows you to pay 1 blood
to untap. Imagine that the card costs 1 blood to play.
There are so many combat situations in which
the Combat Ends is easily worth /more than/ the 1 blood:
the .44, a Brujah with Blur and 3 Undead Strengths,
etc., etc. And even if the card costs 1 blood,
those people who now use 12 would most likely use
at least 6. They're not going to replace them all
with Open Crate's and/or Dodges: they're never the same.
I'd say that making Majesty cost 1 blood to play
(and 1 more to untap if Superior) is at all
reasonable. Opponent used 1 action to Bum's
Rush you, so you have to spend 1 blood
to counter it. Remember that opponent has
to build an entire combat deck to support it
(unlike WwEF, which just goes in about any deck);
you only need a fraction of your deck for
those Majesty's.
Many combat cards cost blood; I'm surprised
why such a useful card as Majesty doesn't.
Making it cost 1 blood is not going to screw
the Ventrue's voting deck with Majesty:
it just helps to balance the cards out.
(Please, no flames against an argument
on restricting Majesty. That is not the
argument here. I'm not talking about restricting
Majesty, I'm talking about making it cost 1 blood.)

Majesty is also one of those highly-demanded cards.

Cards that give a /lot/ of blood, especially
those that can give a lot of pool in combos,
tend to be in great demand. Some ways should be
thought of to limit the use of these cards.
Another post of mine contained some examples,
such as making Minion Tap cost 1 pool (in the least),
limiting Giant's Blood to giving 3 blood, and making
Blood Doll cost nothing to play, but costs
2 vampire blood to get 1 pool. (This would
equate Blood Doll with a Powerbase. The
Blood Doll as it is, is equivalent to
2 Powerbases without a cost to play it.)

Think about making a big vampire, and then Minion
Tap half of its blood (the absolutely most
mundane use of the card). This usage alone
is almost equivalent to playing /many/ skill cards
on a small vampire. No wonder the card is so
much sought after.

It's quite clear that the Ivory Bow's capabilities
should well cost 2 pool (compare with Flamethrower),
but it is designed to be a rare unique card that
motivitates players to buy a lot of cards to
get one, so I won't argue too much about
the case here.

Some general hosers such as Charnas the Imp is also
IMO a bit cheesy. Unlike Muddled Vampire Hunter,
which can easily be neutralized, there is no
good counter for Charnas: the Tremere pays 1 blood,
and the victim is pretty doomed. IMO either the action
to get Charnas should be more blockable, such
as (D) at +0 stealth, or Charnas should cost 2 or 3
blood. Even if it costs 3 blood, a lot of
people are still going to use it (because
it's very difficult to get rid of, once hooked).

The most of all, Fame. Can easily make your
prey lose 3 blood, sometimes repeatedly, without
a cost to play the card.

This is true. But having cards that are overly powerful and
requiring everyone to put them in their deck IMO makes
the game less "colorful", regardless of whether those
cards ar common or rare. Of course, as you tried to say,
if those cards are common, it is not that "evil" (in a
business $$$ sense) as the case when the cards are rare.

>// The problem with over-powerful cards is exactly that everyone
>// is putting those cards in their decks (if they have them)
>// regardless of their overall deck strategy. Any deck
>// without a Minion Tap or 2 (or 4) would not do as well ...

>Very poor example. Most people I've seen around here with successful
>decks occasionally have maybe 1 minion tap (never mind the accepted local
>maximum of 2 of any).

The max of 2 change things a lot. Permanent Intercept become
much more important because neither Auspex/Intercept
nor Obfuscate-Stealth is as effective. It's harder to
build a concentrated deck based on vampire disciplines,
so you don't really need those medium to large vampires.
In that case, players tend to use smaller vampires,
and the number of vampires is more important than their
age, or how many skills they have. Therefore, Minion Tap
is not as effective, and WwEF becomes very important
(because it's hard to build the "I don't wanna block him"
combat deck). See argument below for how Minion Tap
can be used effectively.

Even if you're not aware of it, a global 2-card limit changes
the game a lot. I personally don't prefer any global 2-card
or 4-card or any number limit. If your group dislikes
spoilers, make a list of them and restrict those cards;
it doesn't make sense, IMO, to restrict "Dodge",
"Social Charm", "Thrown Sewer Lid", or "Skin of Rock".
That would just prohibit some interesting decks and
further yet force everybody to use spoilers. Discipline
cards usually work better if you have a fair porportion
of them in the deck, unlike spoilers which usually work
well on its own.

Since my discussions were based on no deck limits other
than those in the basic rules, our opinions had to differ
at times.

>Blood dolls tend to be a more sound choice,
>but you have to decide depending on the deck if you want the quick
>grab, or a slow grab that can also be used to heal the vampire

Yes, Blood Doll is also on my "I want it changed" list.

>More sound examples
>are wwef, KRCG, or sport bikes.

Yes, WwEF is too cheap. Permanent intercept is very handy,
but they cost blood. More specifically, they cost pool.
Auspex-intercept does not cost pool, nor does Obfuscate-stealth,
which counters permanent intercept easily. However, neither
can be used effectively under a 2-card limit. Someone
suggested using Raven Spy's instead of Sports Bikes;
however, if the deck is limited to 2 Raven Spies,
then we'll still need Sports Bikes. The 2-card global
limit not only restricts spoilers, it prohibits many
perfectly innocent strategies and decks from being used.

>However, saying a deck wouldn't do
>as well without 2 (or especially 4) minion taps is silly, I'd have
>to remove a more useful blood card like a short term, or worse
>yet thin out my deck theme cards -- and for a card that gives
>me a one shot suck!

Minion Taps are most useful in decks concentrated in 2 to 4
skills. You bring out a 6 blood vampire, Minion Tap it
for 4, and the result is the equivalent of a 2 blood
vampire with 4 skill cards on it. To build a deck
around Minion Taps (innocent, non-combo use),
find the 6-8 blood vampires with the skills you want,
put a lot of them in your crypt, bring them out,
Minion Tap them and bring out another one. The advantage
of this is that you don't need to use the Master Skill
cards any more. You can take out all the skill cards,
substitute some for Minion taps, and the rest for the
gain blood cards that you mentioned. Of course, an
Information Highway would be really helpful for this
strategy. Such a deck, ideally, will beat a weenie deck
trying to use skill cards, and also a less concentrated
/or/ less balanced deck because its vampires has got
better skills than everybody else. In a 2-card limit
situation where you often got the skill on your
vampire but don't have the right cards in your hand
to use the skill effectively, this strategy has lost
its purpose. Also, this strategy, limited to
2 Minion Taps in the deck, cannot be used reliably,
as are many other strategies, under such restriction.

Investment Cards (such as Short Term) are more favored
in less concentrated decks where cards are sometimes
unplayable and cards cycle slowly. In a Brujah combat
deck where combat cards drop like flies, if you use
the same proportion of Master cards (the /must have/
spoilers), you'll end up with more master cards in your
hand than you can play, and you don't really want to
sacrifice 4 master phases to gain 2 pool.

>I'll play my current set a blood cards which
>has blood dolls which can suck blood to me from all kinds of
>continuous blood sources instead, it may be slow, but I've see
>5 blood easily syphoned in a turn without a minion tap...

It is also harder to counter spoilers effectively
under a 2-card limit. No Bum's Rush+Haven Uncovered
combat deck to Torporize the Blood Doll, and also
only 2 Arsons in the deck to take out locations ...

a strike: combat ends counters an entire
deck strategy with one card. Against an effective
combat deck, this single card can very often (too often)
make the difference between escaping unscatched and
Torpor. If you can't strike: combat ends, to escape
from Torpor from a Celerity-rich enemy, you'll
need a Dodge, a lot of Open Crate's,
and would still take up to 8 damage from
2 additional strikes in the first round, which
you can't Dodge without an additional strike
yourself.

I know, when you have a 2-card limit, cards such as Blur
may become a precious resource; but here my discussion
has always been no card limits, so what strike: combat
ends is countering is not the actual Blur card, but
the /Sequence of Play/ opportunity to play the
Blur. In a deck with 9 or more Blur cards, it's
not the card that matters, but the Seq. of Play
/opportunity/ to play that card and send your
opponent to Torpor.

addressing (and calls for even stricter card limits).

> concerned about what your opponent is going to do to

Not without a 2-card limit. A deck with 16 .44's will
stand absolutely /no chance/ against a well-constructed
Brujah or Gangrel combat deck; a deck with 16 Majesty
may escape unscatched.

As I mentioned again and again, a 2-card limit puts the
emphasis of the game resource on cards (which I believe
is contrary to the original intent of the design)
and makes "permanents" much more valuable. if you can
have as many as one type of cards as you want, it's not
the card themselves, but other game resources (blood,
ready minions, Sequence of Play) that becomes the
main constraint of what you can or cannot do, the
cards being supplementary rather than the center of the
constraint (cf. MtG).

>(2) the Brujah -- if he drops all 4 cards on the table at once and plays
> them he deserves to lose the damage. You should
> always wait to see your opponent's strike before
> adding additional strikes or using things like

Wait here. It is /illegal/ to play additional strike cards, the
strike cards for the additional strikes, and Press cards
if your opponent plays a Majesty. The Brujah is making
an /illegal/ play if he tries to put down 4 cards at once.
He should be stopped, and his illegally played cards
should be put back into his hand. He /cannot/ draw
new cards to replace them.

In games with well-constructed concentrated decks (without
any card restrictions), what the Brujah is worrying
about is /not/ the combat cards that he's spending,
but the precious opportunity of getting his opponent
into a fight with him, which almost always means
torporization of his poor opponent, barring a Majesty.

One very fundamental difference between Jyhad and MtG
is that, in Jyhad, (library) cards are replaced as soon as they
are played, and are not drawn unless cards have been
played or discarded. This means that, basically, playing
cards (except rare ones) does not really use up a
player's resources; the cards function more as
opportunities that allow the player to more fully
utilize the other game resources (blood, ready minions,
Sequence of Play), which are not replenished as readily
as a played card.

Deck restrictions tend to thwart this fundamental
concept, hence I don't suggest playing with them
(at least, not playing with a global limit, which
restricts non-spoilers necessary for many strategies).

inevitable.

allows for situation when everyone has about the same strength, and is just
sitting there, to be broken. Once someone's vampires start tapping, then his
predator starts to do things, then his predator's predator can afford to do
things, etc.

busy to be availiable to support existing products.

The problem with gross combos is that it rules out lots of
other `normal' strategies as inferior, and greatly limits
freedom of the player to create his own strategy. It also
makes careful planning and playing unnecessary; all it takes
to win now is luck to draw, play and counter those combos.

I have no problem with the Claws -> Amaranth combo, because
there are so many drawbacks and restrictions, and normal ways
to counter it. I do have problem with Fame combos and
Minion Tap -> Hospitality combos. These combos have little
to do with the rest of the game system (unlike Claws, which
is tied into combat), are not based on a deck theme
(as Claws is), and takes much more specific measures to counter.

Potence/Celerity `combo' deck, and a Fame/Day Op. `combo' deck.
Maybe it's just me. Also, as stated in my article, a lot of
Jyhad is on allocating deck proportions. MtG "/is/ a competition
to see who draws better sooner"; Jyhad is more on allocating
deck proportions. With a `good' deck, you /don't/ need
too much luck to get the cards you want. If you want a
WwEF in your hand all the time, put 12 or 15 in your deck.

It takes a lot of careful calculations and evaluations to
balance out the proportions of each card in a `good' deck;
it doesn't take much, other than 6th grade intellience
and in some cases $$$, to build a deck loaded with
annoying combos (ever beaten by a $$$ rich 13-yr-old
in MtG?) . To illustrate the former point, consider the
degenerate Majesty-bleed Ventrue deck I posted. There are
players who, based on their misconceptions, thought that I
should not have put any "Threats" card in the deck.
But the fact is, at that proportion of Dominate bleeders
in the deck, "Conditioning" cards may jam the hand,
and in /that/ deck "Threats" have its place. Even
with a degenerate deck, there are some delicate
issues that must be taken care of concerning
the delicate balance of similar cards in the deck.
However, with some of the gross combos, their use
is much more obvious than the use of "Threats" in my
degenerate deck.

And, up to this day, no one has pointed out to me that,
for /that/ deck, its effectiveness can be slightly
improved by replacing yet some "Conditioning" with
"Legal Manipulations". Since you burn Presence
cards on every bleed action but burn Dominate
cards only on unblocked ones, it follows that you
need more Presence bleed cards than Dominate
for maximum bleed effectiveness, with /that/
proportion of bleed cards in the
deck. Also, that deck is more centered on Presence
than on Dominate to begin with.

as we know it. If there are lots of (or even a few)
spoilers, much of the significance of that work
would be taken out.

design of the game. If the game allows a "morally wrong"
deck to win easily, the game should be fixed. Sid Meier
did that with his computer game, "Civilization", to
stop the "Barbarian Horde" strategy. I know of many games
that are "degeneracy proof". I know, in my heart, that
you can make a CCG as close to "degeneracy proof" as possible.
Jyhad is pretty close, but isn't quite making it yet. But it
seems to me that nobody is doing anything, or wants to.

cost of 3 - that's too steep - I'm just using it
